_why: The DECLARED state of the whole GitHub surface. scripts/ghaudit.py compares this to the live API and exits non-zero on a difference. Before this file that state was typed into SECURITY.md with a date beside it: true when written, unfalsifiable later, stale without saying so. A declaration a machine can compare is the only kind that cannot rot quietly — and the reverse direction matters most, because it is what catches a webhook, an environment or a merge setting added through the UI and recorded nowhere.

secret_scanning_non_provider_patterns.blocked_by: MEASURED at v1.3.0: PATCH /repos/{repo} with this field returns HTTP 200 and changes nothing, and /user/code-security/configurations returns 404 for this account. The toggle belongs to GitHub Secret Protection, which this user-owned repository does not carry (security_and_analysis.advanced_security is null). Re-measure with `python scripts/ghaudit.py`; it becomes a DIFF the moment the platform grants it.

secret_scanning_validity_checks.blocked_by: Same gate as non-provider patterns, measured the same way at v1.3.0: a 200 that does nothing. Not a blind spot and not an oversight — a platform entitlement this account does not have.

ruleset.name: main-protection
ruleset._checks_note: These are CHECK RUN names — a job's `name:` — not workflow names. A ruleset naming a check that never reports blocks every merge, so `Atlas CI` (the workflow) would wedge the branch while `Contract` (its job) gates it. MEASURED at v1.3.0 on pull request #2: Contract, Dependency Review, Analyze (python) and Analyze (actions) all reported and passed, which is the evidence for requiring the two CodeQL contexts. The failure on pull request #1 came from a stale branch carrying a deleted advanced CodeQL workflow, not from default setup.

_not_required_yet.Supply-chain hygiene: OpenSSF Scorecard runs on push and on a schedule, never on a pull request, so it cannot be a merge gate. Requiring it would name a context that never reports.

ruleset._bypass_note: EMPTY ON PURPOSE, and it is the change with the most consequence in this file. The ruleset previously granted repository admins an always-bypass, so every rule was advisory for the one actor most likely to be in a hurry — and Scorecard's branch-protection check says so in as many words: 'branch protection settings apply to administrators' is disabled. Direct pushes to main now fail for everyone; the lane-plus-pull-request flow is unaffected because zero approvals are required, so a solo maintainer can still merge their own work. Reverting is one call: PUT .../rulesets/23838023 with bypass_actors set back to the RepositoryRole id 5 entry.
ruleset._parameters_note: WHY THESE ARE DECLARED FIELD BY FIELD. A PUT to the rulesets API replaces the rule it names and leaves out what the payload omits, so a partial payload silently reverts parameters it never mentions. That happened: a 'revert the bypass' call built from an older payload left bypass_actors untouched and switched dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push and required_review_thread_resolution back off — two Scorecard branch-protection points, lost with no error and no diff. ghaudit compared the rule TYPES and the required checks, so it reported 'ok' over the regression: a roster that checks a name and not its content. Every parameter this repository depends on is now compared individually.

settings._settings_note: allow_merge_commit is FALSE because the ruleset requires linear history: a merge method the UI offers and the rules refuse is an affordance that produces a failed push and no explanation. delete_branch_on_merge is TRUE because a finished lane with ahead=0 is debris by this repository's own worktree rules. has_wiki is FALSE because the wiki lives in-tree at wiki/, under the same contract as everything else — a second, unversioned wiki is a duplicate surface where one copy goes stale and no reader can tell which is live. allow_auto_merge is TRUE because push and merge are ONE step here (branchstate.py --land): a pull request merges the moment its required checks pass, so no lane sits pushed-and-stranded waiting on somebody to remember it. It was live on the platform and declared nowhere until 2.27.0 — a setting the audit could not see.

webhooks._webhooks_note: Zero, and checked in both directions. A webhook is an outbound data path: one added through the UI and recorded nowhere is the shape this audit exists to catch.

environments._environments_note: Both were created by GitHub features rather than by a deployment, and both hold zero secrets and zero variables — verified per environment, because an environment is exactly where a secret hides from a repository-level scan. This repository deploys nothing, so an environment that acquires a secret is a finding, not a configuration.

scorecard._scorecard_note: A RATCHET, AND IT IS PER CHECK. The aggregate hides which check fell: Branch-Protection can drop three points while Pinned-Dependencies rises three and the total does not move, so a single floor would have reported that as fine. Every check carries its own floor, measured at contract v2.0.0, and ghaudit reports each one that is below it. Raising a floor must name what earned the rise. docs/CERTIFICATION.md carries, per check, what would raise it and whether that is owner action or structural. Checks scoring -1 (Packaging, Signed-Releases) are INCONCLUSIVE rather than failing — nothing is published to a package index — so they carry no floor and are named in the document instead of being quietly counted as passes. Branch-Protection was raised at v2.2.0 by removing the administrator bypass, dismissing stale reviews on push and requiring review threads to be resolved; the remaining points each need a second person to approve a pull request, which docs/CERTIFICATION.md records as structural.
scorecard._open_shortfall: NONE OPEN. SAST closed at v2.27.0 — measured 10, 'SAST tool is run on all commits', after reporting 8 from v2.0.0 while it healed. It was REPORTED and never lowered: the scan's own words were '4 commits out of 5 are checked', the unchecked commit predated the pull-request flow, and CodeQL analyses what arrives through a pull request. LOWERING THE FLOOR TO MAKE THE ROW GREEN WOULD HAVE TURNED A RATCHET INTO A RECORD OF WHATEVER HAPPENED LAST, which is the one thing a ratchet exists to prevent. It is also the case that justified the per-check design: the aggregate ROSE from 5.9 to 6.5 in the same measurement that left SAST short.
_ratchet_log: 5.9 at v2.0.0 — the first measurement, taken as the floor
6.5 at v2.2.0 — actions pinned to commit SHAs, the pip install hash-pinned, the administrator bypass removed, stale reviews dismissed and review threads required

6.7 at v2.4.0 — Pinned-Dependencies reached 10 ('all dependencies are pinned') and Security-Policy reached 10 once the policy carried a reachable advisory link. Both floors were raised to match, because a ratchet that does not follow the measurement up is just a number somebody typed once.

7.3 at v2.6.0 — Fuzzing reached 10 once ClusterFuzzLite was detected and Signed-Releases reached 10 on the first attested artifact. IN THE SAME SCAN, Pinned-Dependencies FELL from 10 to 7: the ClusterFuzzLite Dockerfile pinned its base image by tag. The aggregate rose and a check fell in one measurement, which is the case the per-check floor exists for — a single floor on the total would have called it an improvement. Fixed at v2.6.1 by pinning the image to its digest.

7.5 at v2.7.0 — eleven checks at 10 (Fuzzing and Signed-Releases among them, both moved by engineering this session) and Pinned-Dependencies back to 10 after the unpinned pip command was deleted rather than pinned. Floors raised to match. The five still open are Code-Review and Contributors (a second person), CII-Best-Practices (one sign-in), Maintained (the repository's age), and Branch-Protection, which is at the ceiling a solo repository can reach.

7.5 at v2.27.0 — SAST reached 10 and its floor rose to match, closing the last shortfall that was healing. The aggregate did not move, which is the point of a per-check ratchet: four checks sit at 0 and one at 4, and every one of them is now recorded with its MECHANISM and its OWNER. Three need a second person or the calendar; one needs a single sign-in. None needs code.

_open_arms.Fuzzing: AT 10 since v2.6.0. ClusterFuzzLite fuzzes fuzz/fuzz_manifest_entry.py for 120 seconds per pull request in code-change mode; the same target runs as a fixed 35-input corpus in Atlas CI wherever atheris is absent, and examples/go carries FuzzPool for the bounded worker pool. The Go target alone did NOT move the check: Scorecard's Go detection is gated on the repository's prominent language, and this tree is Markdown and Python — measured, not assumed.
_open_arms.Signed-Releases: AT 10 since v2.5.0: '1 out of the last 1 releases have a total of 1 signed artifacts'. Every release since carries a deterministic tarball, its digest and a signed in-toto bundle; `gh attestation verify` exits 0 and the published digest equals the computed one, both checked rather than assumed.
_open_arms.Code-Review: STRUCTURAL, AND THE MECHANISM IS A PERSON. Measured at v2.27.0: 0 of 9 changesets approved. Every change goes through a pull request with four required checks, but Scorecard counts APPROVING REVIEWS and GitHub does not let an author approve their own. The only mechanisms are a second human reviewer or a review account, and a review account controlled by the sole maintainer would raise the number while approving nothing — this repository refuses to manufacture a supply-chain trust signal. Sole remedy: invite a reviewer.
_open_arms.Contributors: STRUCTURAL: needs contributors from two or more organisations.
_open_arms.CII-Best-Practices: OWNER ACTION, AND IT IS THE ONLY ZERO WITH A MECHANISM THAT NEEDS NO SECOND PERSON. Register the project at bestpractices.dev and answer the criteria; the answers are already mapped in config/openssf-best-practices.json and docs/CERTIFICATION.md, and most are satisfied by controls this audit already verifies live. It is a form, not work, and it needs a sign-in this repository cannot perform on the owner's behalf.
_open_arms.Maintained: TIME, AND NOTHING ELSE. The scan's own words: 'project was created within the last 90 days'. It clears itself. Committing to hurry it would be activity manufactured for a metric.
_open_arms.Branch-Protection: AT THE CEILING A SOLO REPOSITORY CAN REACH, and the remaining tiers are the same gap as Code-Review. On: deletion, force-push, linear history, a required pull request, four required checks, up-to-date branches, stale-review dismissal, thread resolution, and no bypass actor. MEASURED at v2.27.0: 4 of 10. Scorecard's tiers 3 to 5 need required_approving_review_count >= 1, code-owner review and last-push approval. Setting any of them on a single-maintainer repository has exactly two outcomes, both worse than the 4: every merge wedges, because nobody can approve; or a bypass actor is added to unwedge it, and a control with a bypass is a declared control that enforces nothing. It moves the day a second reviewer exists, not before.
_open_arms.SAST: AT 10 since v2.27.0: 'SAST tool is run on all commits'. It healed exactly as predicted once five consecutive commits had landed through pull requests, which is the evidence that the REPORT-DO-NOT-LOWER response to a shortfall was the right one.
_open_arms.Packaging: DECLINED, with the reason: nothing here is published to a package index, which pyproject.toml states explicitly. An inconclusive check is excluded from the aggregate; a publish workflow for a repository that publishes nothing would be a skeleton.

check_weights._weights_note: OpenSSF Scorecard's documented risk tiers — Critical 10, High 7.5, Medium 5, Low 2.5 — declared here so `ghaudit.py` can say what closing each arm is WORTH instead of a document guessing. The model is checked against the live aggregate on every run: if the computed value disagrees with the published one, the weights are wrong and the audit says so rather than projecting from a broken model.

releases._releases_note: A version with no tag is a claim with no artifact; a tag with no release is an artifact nobody can find. The release procedure in docs/VERSIONING.md ends here. MEASURED at 2.27.0: releases stopped at v2.8.0 while the contract reached 2.27.0, so the README's version badge showed v2.8.0 for nineteen versions. Versions 2.9.0 to 2.26.0 were never tagged and are NOT back-filled — tagging old commits now would invent release history; their changes are in docs/VERSIONING.md. branchstate.py --sync tags main's VERSION after a merge, and this row fails whenever the latest release trails it.

_description_note: The GitHub description carries NO count. It said '29 language routes' while the atlas routed 34 — the same defect as a number typed into prose, on the surface a reader sees before the README.

code_scanning._code_scanning_note: CodeQL default setup selects languages by Linguist detection, so making the examples detectable expanded it to Swift — and Analyze (swift) fails: CodeQL must BUILD Swift, and autobuild cannot build a single file that needs `swiftc -parse-as-library`. Swift is excluded in .gitattributes with the trigger to reverse it (a Package.swift). Rust and C/C++ are not selectable by default setup at all, which the API says in as many words. The example itself is still exercised: `exrun.py` compiles and runs it on any machine with swiftc, and that is a stronger check than a scan that never completes.
